title: Erase-While-Iterating, Correctly
statement:
`std::vector<int>::erase(it)` removes the element `it` points to and
returns an iterator to whatever now sits in its place -- the element that
used to come *after* it. That return value matters more than it looks
like it should: a hand-written loop that calls `erase` and then blindly
advances its own iterator afterwards skips the element that just slid
into the gap, silently, with no warning and no crash.

## Your function

```
void RemoveMultiplesOf(std::vector<int>& values, int n);
```

`n` is always at least `1`. **Mutate `values` in place**, removing every
element that is a multiple of `n` (including `0`, which is a multiple of
everything), and keeping the relative order of everything that survives.
`values` may be empty.

## Watch out

- **A loop shaped like `for (auto it = values.begin(); it !=
  values.end(); ++it) { if (cond) values.erase(it); }` skips the element
  right after every one it removes.** `erase(it)` already advances past
  the removed element, to the one that now occupies its old position --
  the loop's own `++it` then moves *past that one too*, and it is never
  checked. Two adjacent multiples of `n` are the case this shows up on:
  the first is removed correctly, and the second, right behind it, is
  skipped and survives even though it should not.
- **The standard fix is the erase-remove idiom**: `std::remove_if`
  rearranges the surviving elements to the front of the vector (in one
  linear pass) and returns an iterator to where the leftovers begin; a
  single call to `values.erase(...)` with that iterator and `values.end()`
  then drops them all in one O(n) operation, no per-element iterator
  bookkeeping required.
- **`0 % n` is always `0`.** A `values` containing `0` should have every
  `0` removed regardless of what `n` is -- there is no need, and no
  correct reason, to special-case it.

every element is a multiple -- the result is empty
two adjacent multiples -- the classic skip-after-erase bug
